lesson.title: What Fraction Is Whose: Mole Fraction in Gas Mixtures
lesson.summary: Mole fraction is the ratio of moles of one component to the total moles in a mixture, and for gases it equals the same component's share of the total pressure, giving a direct link between composition and partial pressure.
lesson.body:
Mole fraction, given the symbol chi (written as the Greek letter chi with a subscript for the substance), is defined simply as the moles of one component divided by the total moles of everything in the mixture: chi_A = n_A / n_total. It is a pure ratio with no units, always a number between 0 and 1, and the mole fractions of every component in a mixture always add up to exactly 1, since together they account for the whole sample.

For gas mixtures specifically, mole fraction has a second meaning that makes it especially useful: because every gas in an ideal mixture shares the same volume and temperature, and partial pressure is directly proportional to moles under those shared conditions (P = nRT/V, and RT/V is the same constant for every gas in the mixture), the mole fraction of a gas equals its partial pressure divided by the total pressure. In symbols, chi_A = n_A/n_total = P_A/P_total. This means you can find a gas's mole fraction either from mole data or from pressure data, whichever you happen to have.

Return to the nitrogen and oxygen mixture from the Dalton's law chapter: 0.10 mol N2 and 0.20 mol O2 in a 5.00 L container at 300 K, for a total of 0.30 mol. Using the mole-based definition: chi(N2) = n(N2)/n_total = 0.10/0.30 = 0.333, and chi(O2) = 0.20/0.30 = 0.667. As expected, 0.333 + 0.667 = 1.00. Now check this using the pressure-based definition instead, using the partial pressures calculated earlier (0.493 atm for N2 and 1.48 atm total): chi(N2) = P(N2)/P_total = 0.493/1.48 = 0.333. Both methods give the same mole fraction, exactly as the relationship chi_A = n_A/n_total = P_A/P_total predicts.

Mole fraction shows up constantly beyond pure gas-law problems, including in solution chemistry and in calculating partial pressures directly from a known composition: if you know the mole fraction of a gas and the total pressure, you can find its partial pressure immediately with P_A = chi_A times P_total, without needing to know the container's volume or temperature at all, since those details are already baked into the total pressure measurement.
